title: Smale’s seventh problem
formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.
status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No general deterministic polynomial-time construction with logarithmic total-energy excess was located. The March 2026 finite-cardinality classification and existing distributional energy guarantees do not establish the uniform algorithmic target. This source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 13 September 2026; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Smale specifies polynomial time in N in the real-number model and universal logarithmic excess energy.
The low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution attains logarithmic excess in expectation and with high probability; efficient generation is a separate issue.
The generalized Diamond ensemble covers every N with an explicit asymptotic expected-energy estimate.
A central limit theorem identifies \(\sqrt{N}\) energy fluctuations for random polynomial zeros.
Revised algebraic classification handles at most six points in all dimensions and a restricted seven-point case.

importance.reason: Smale's seventh problem asks for efficient construction of globally near-optimal configurations.

category_assignment.reason: Category from the approved fundamental-problem proposal

definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.

sentences: Smale's seventh problem concerns placing N points on the unit sphere so that their logarithmic interaction energy is nearly minimal.
The target is an algorithm running in time polynomial in N.
Its output energy may exceed the global minimum by only a universal constant times log N.
This is an additive energy guarantee, which requires more precise control than merely producing visually well-distributed points.
A construction with a rigorous bound would connect efficient computation with the equilibrium behavior of many mutually repelling particles on a curved surface.

references.title: Mathematical Problems for the Next Century
references.locator: Problem 7; real-number computation model and logarithmic excess energy.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?
